assumptions.label: Typical easement (right-of-way) width, 115 kV line (Georgia Transmission)
assumptions.section: Typical Transmission Line Easement Widths (approximates) - Roadside | Cross Country
assumptions.exactExcerpt: 115 kV Line Single pole 25-42.5 feet + 100 feet
assumptions.note: Georgia Transmission Corp. fact sheet (2017). The two values are the Roadside and Cross Country columns. Typical is the cross-country width, which the sheet prints as '+ 100 feet'; I read that as 100 ft or more. Low is the roadside easement (25-42.5 ft), used where the line runs next to a road right-of-way. The H-frame row also says '+ 100 feet' cross-country. No source gives a high value. As a cross-check, MISO's indicative width is 90 ft (rowWidthFt.115.miso). I found no public DESC or Georgia Power statement of a 115 kV width.

assumptions.label: Typical right-of-way width, 230 kV line (DESC / SCE&G certificate application)
assumptions.section: Application, SC PSC Docket 2010-238-E - line description (Denny Terrace-Pineland 230 kV)
assumptions.exactExcerpt: WIDTH OF RIGHT-OF-WAY: 100 FEET (Typical) DESIGN VOLTAGE: 230 kV
assumptions.note: South Carolina Electric & Gas (now Dominion Energy South Carolina) filed this Siting Act application for an 8.0-mile 230 kV line in northeast Columbia in 2010. It gives 100 ft as the typical width. Georgia Transmission gives 100 ft (single pole) to 125 ft (H-frame) cross-country (rowWidthFt.230.gtc). MISO's indicative width is 125 ft (rowWidthFt.230.miso).

assumptions.label: Easement width, 230 kV line, Georgia Transmission range (roadside / single pole / H-frame)
assumptions.section: Typical Transmission Line Easement Widths (approximates)
assumptions.exactExcerpt: 230 kV Line Single pole 25-42.5 feet + 100 feet 230 kV Line H-frame n/a + 125 feet
assumptions.note: Low is the roadside single-pole easement (25-42.5 ft). Typical is the cross-country single-pole width ('+ 100 feet'). High is the cross-country H-frame width ('+ 125 feet'). The sheet says these values are approximate.

assumptions.label: Easement width, 500 kV steel lattice line (Georgia Transmission)
assumptions.section: Typical Transmission Line Easement Widths (approximates) - Cross Country
assumptions.exactExcerpt: 500 kV Steel Lattice Structure n/a 150-180 feet
assumptions.note: The sheet gives a range of 150-180 ft cross-country and no roadside value. Typical is set to the low end of the published range (150 ft) so the estimate stays conservative; I did not compute a midpoint. The 100-150 ft figure in the structure-height table on the same page is a pole height, not a width. MISO's indicative width is 200 ft (rowWidthFt.500.miso). I found no DESC 500 kV width in public sources.

assumptions.label: Right-of-way land priced at full USDA-based land value (MISO planning convention)
assumptions.unit: fraction of land value per acre
assumptions.section: 2. Right-of-Way, Land Acquisition, and Regulatory and Permitting (printed page 6)
assumptions.exactExcerpt: MISO utilizes the annual USDA Land Values summary to estimate the value of pastureland
assumptions.note: This is a planning convention, not an observed ratio of easement price to fee value. On the same page MISO says 'All land costs are based upon the acreage of land that the new transmission line would traverse' (also verified, page 7). Table 2.1 on page 8 then prices right-of-way per acre at the land value (pasture; crop = 3x pasture; urban = 5x pasture), with no easement discount, so the implied share is 1.0. A separate right-of-way acquisition cost per acre is added on top (rowAcquisitionCostPerAcre). Use as a default only with that explanation. No SC or GA source states a typical share.

assumptions.label: Example easement payment as a share of land value (Grain Belt Express, Missouri 2016)
assumptions.unit: fraction of average fee value per acre
assumptions.section: Compensation Calculation - Easement Payment
assumptions.exactExcerpt: Clean Line will pay 110% of the average value of the land, based on recent sales in the county
assumptions.note: This is one developer's landowner offer, filed with the Missouri PSC as Schedule DKL-3 in June 2016, for a merchant HVDC line with an easement about 150-200 ft wide. It is not SC or GA and not a typical utility share. It is only evidence that easement payments can match or exceed fee value, so use it only as a high sensitivity case.

assumptions.label: New single-circuit 115 kV line, exploratory cost per mile (MISO; Mississippi as Southeast proxy)
assumptions.section: Table 4.1-1: Exploratory cost estimate - AC transmission, new single circuit transmission line $/mile (printed page 38)
assumptions.note: The columns are 69 / 115 / 138 / 161 / 230 / 345 / 500 / 765 kV (header verified on the same page), so Mississippi 115 kV = $2.2M/mile. SC and GA are not MISO states; I used Mississippi as the closest Southeast proxy, and that choice is mine, not the source's. Low and high span all 15 states in the table: $1.8M (Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota) to $2.2M (Louisiana, Mississippi, Texas). The table footnote reads 'Includes contingency (30%) and AFUDC (7.5%)'. Page 2 says data are in 2023 dollars 'escalated ... to 2024 U.S. dollars at a rate of 5%'. MTEP24 is the latest edition I could verify that prints the $/mile tables in the PDF; the MTEP26 guide moves its tables to a separate workbook (see costEscalationPerYear).

assumptions.label: DESC plan example: Stevens Creek-Graniteville 115 kV rebuild, total cost / stated miles
assumptions.section: Project 49 of 54 - Stevens Creek - Graniteville 115 kV: Rebuild (Project ID 6809 T)

assumptions.note: Derived: $18,200,000 / 15 miles = ~$1.21M/mile. The total comes from the same page, verified separately with the excerpt 'Total $18,200,000' (FOUND on page 49). assumptions.label: DESC plan example: Jasper-Okatie 230 kV #2 new line, total cost / stated miles

assumptions.exactExcerpt: building them at the same time will avoid the need to mobilize construction crews twice to work on the same structures and thereby will reduce construction costs
assumptions.note: This is qualitative. SCE&G (now DESC) testified that building two lines together avoids mobilizing crews twice, which is one avoided mobilization. The case involved the St. George segment and Lake Murray line, which share right-of-way and structures. No dollar amount or percentage is given. It applies only when the projects share work sites or structures, which no source establishes for any DESC-Georgia Power pair. That limit belongs in the UI.

unresolved: easementShare (plain key) is left out on purpose. No public DESC, Georgia Power, Santee Cooper, Georgia Transmission, or SC/GA state source states a typical easement price as a share of fee value. The Georgia Power ROW brochure (gpc-row-brochure, page 2, verified: 'The majority of our rights-of-way are in the form of easements') and Georgia Power's land-acquisition web page give no ratio; both say compensation is evaluated property by property. Georgia Transmission's 'Private Property, Public Use' brochure refers only to fair market value. Wisconsin PSC and DATCP easement brochures give no ratio either. Instead I supplied two documented conventions under separate keys: easementShare.misoConvention (MISO prices right-of-way at full USDA-based land value, 1.0) and easementShare.cleanLineMO (one developer's 110% offer in Missouri, 2016). Suggested UI default: compute avoided right-of-way land at full USDA value per acre (the MISO convention) and label it that way.

mobilizationShare is not supplied. I found no credible public utility, regulator, or RTO source that gives mobilization, shared-outage, or crew-coordination savings as a percent of project cost. What does exist: (a) MISO's MTEP 2018 fixed mobilization/demobilization unit cost per line project, $100k at 115 kV, $200k at 230 kV and $300k at 500 kV in 2018 dollars (mobilizationCostPerProject.*); and (b) SCE&G/DESC testimony in SC PSC Docket 2011-325-E that building two lines on shared structures at the same time avoids mobilizing crews twice (avoidedMobilizations = 1, qualitative, no dollar value). Nothing public quantifies shared-outage savings.

I found no public source stating DESC's 115 kV or 500 kV right-of-way widths. The Dominion Energy SC right-of-way brochure and easement guidelines (dominionenergy.com, SC PDFs) give no voltage-specific widths. The Santee Cooper project pages I checked also gave none. The 115 and 500 kV widths therefore come from Georgia Transmission, with MISO as a cross-check.

I found no published cost-per-mile guide for the Southeast (SC, GA, or SERTP). The Georgia Power IRP public disclosure and the SERTP plan give no unit costs. The per-mile values here are MISO-footprint values (Mississippi as proxy), plus DESC-derived ratios (project total / stated miles) that include non-line scope and are single-project figures, not unit costs.

The MISO MTEP26 guide (June 10, 2026) keeps its $/mile and right-of-way tables in a companion xlsx workbook that fetch_source.py and find_excerpt.py cannot verify. I therefore quoted the MTEP24 PDF tables (2024 $) and the MTEP26 statement of 4% escalation. The MTEP25 guide URL now returns 403. MTEP24 page 2 says data are 'in 2023 U.S. dollars' escalated to 2024 at 5%, so the dollar year is slightly ambiguous; I treat it as 2024 $.

USDA NASS table excerpts are column-ordered runs of numbers, because the default pdftotext output reads each table one column at a time. Each note gives the row order (Southeast, Alabama, Florida, Georgia, South Carolina) and year. The UI should show the section title and page so a judge can see which row each value is.

Page numbers for the MISO guides are PDF page indexes, which is what find_excerpt and the audit use. The printed page numbers are one lower (e.g. PDF p39 = printed p38) and are given in each section field.

Not retrieved: the USDA Rural Development FONSI for the East Central Georgia Reliability Project (rd.usda.gov served an HTML block page instead of the PDF). It might contain Georgia Transmission right-of-way widths or costs for an east-Georgia project.
